newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open unchanged before jobless data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open unchanged before jobless data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened scarcely changed on Thursday ahead of weekly jobless claims data and the March personal income and spending report.
Trading was light overseas with much of Europe and Asia closed for the May 1 Labor Day holiday.
European debt markets were firm, in line with gains in U.S. bonds over the last two days, analysts said.
The benchmark 30-year bond was unchanged at 95-26/32, yielding 6.96 percent, in early trade. Two-year notes were down 1/32 to to 100-5/32, yielding 6.29 percent.
New jobless claims for the week ended April 26 are likely to total 325,000, up from 324,000 a week earlier, economists told Reuters.

Personal income is expected to be up 0.4 percent for March after a 0.9 percent February gain and personal consumption is expected to be up 0.5 percent for March after a 0.3 percent rise in February, according to an average forecast provided by economists in a Reuters poll.
Traders said the data are not likely to be big market movers with April payroll employment data due in 24 hours.

What could move the market is the closely watched April National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) survey, due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. The April NAPM index is expected to be down slightly to 53.6 from 55.0 in March, according to economists polled by Reuters. A reading above 50 indicates an expanding economy.

The NAPM survey is due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT. And at the same time, the market will get what are likely to be less influential March construction spending figures. These are expected to show that spending slipped 0.2 percent in March after jumping 2.3 percent in February.

A friendly NAPM reading could push the market higher but some cautiousness before the April employment report could limit gains, even though the market does not expect the Labor Department's April report to be especially threatening.

Economists, on average, look for April payroll growth of 211,000 jobs with an unemployment rate stable at 5.2 percent, average hourly earnings up 0.3 percent and the length of the avrage workweek slightly shortened to 34.7 hours in April from 34.8 hours in March.
In early trade, three-month bill rates were one basis point lower at 5.10 percent. Six-month and year-bill rates were each unchanged at 5.31 percent and 5.57 percent, respectively.
Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 100-5/32, yielding 6.29 percent. Five-year notes were unchanged at 100-7/32, yielding 6.57 percent. Ten-year notes were up 1/32 to 96-22/32, yielding 6.72 percent.
